extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy and intellectual history (scholars, graduate students, educated general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level historical analysis of moral ideas and institutions in the pagan (Greek and Roman) world, contrasting schools (Stoics, Epicureans, Peripatetics) and assessing social causes that shaped moral types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic ethical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Stoics asserted two cardinal principles—that virtue was the sole legitimate object to be aspired to, and that it involved so complete an ascendancy of the reason as altogether to extinguish the affections.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoicism holds virtue as the only true good and demands rational control to suppress passions; the text treats this as the defining standard of Stoic moral excellence and the source of its austere ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripatetic/Platonist moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripatetics and many philosophers derived from Plato "admitted that virtue was an object wholly distinct from interest, and that it should be the leading motive of life; but they maintained that happiness was also a good, and a certain regard for it legitimate. They admitted that virtue consisted in the supremacy of the reason over the affections, but they allowed the exercise of the latter within restricted limits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moderate standard balances reason and affections and accepts happiness as a secondary good; used as a corrective to Stoic excesses in evaluating ethical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive: virtue leads to prosperity (prudential/theological argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral teachers may argue that "the disposition of events is such that prosperity will attend a virtuous life, and adversity a vicious one"—a proposition dependent on theological tenets or social organisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion evaluates moral teaching by its claim that virtue is instrumentally rewarded (in this world or by providence); its force depends on belief in providence and societal conditions that link virtue to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive: virtue as health of the mind (Plato's model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vice is to the mind what disease is to the body, and a state of virtue is in consequence a state of health; a well-ordered mind may be valued for its own sake, independently of external goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard assesses virtue as intrinsic psychological well-being rather than external reward; favourable to sustained self-culture and habitual moral formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive: pleasure from performing virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that a distinct sensation of pleasure follows the deliberate performance of a virtuous act (the 'luxury of doing good'), especially strong in benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates moral systems by the immediate emotional satisfaction virtue produces; treats moral action's hedonic payoff as a motivating criterion distinct from broader happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive: duty as an independent natural motive (intuitive school)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intuitive school asserts that "the notion of duty furnishes in itself a natural motive of action of the highest order, wholly distinct from all the refinements and modifications of self-interest... Men feel that a certain course of life is the natural end of their being, and they feel bound, even at the expense of happiness, to pursue it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion measures moral systems by whether they appeal to an internal, non-instrumental sense of duty that can motivate action irrespective of consequences or beliefs about rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical/didactic method (use of exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient moralists commonly used history and biography didactically: "One of the first tasks of every moralist was to collect traits of character illustrating the precepts he enforced," exemplified by Valerius Maximus and Plutarch's emphasis on emulating great men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates moral instruction by reliance on historical exemplars: virtue taught through model lives and imitation rather than abstract rules; effectiveness judged by cultural relevance and accessibility of examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: National character determines moral type
rubrics_metrics.description: The circumstances of a people "tended inevitably to the production of a certain type of character"—e.g., Rome's military, patriotic society predisposed it toward Stoicism rather than Epicureanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for assessing moral doctrines: whether they align with, arise from, or are reinforced by national social conditions (warfare, institutions, family structure). Moral ideals are judged in relation to sociopolitical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: War and patriotism as formative schools of heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: War is described as 'the great school of heroism' that 'teaches men how to die' and develops self-sacrifice, discipline, and the subordination of personal wishes to the society—conditions that produced Roman heroic virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the origins and plausibility of heroic moral types by examining social practices (military service, patriotism) that cultivate such virtues; treats institutional context as causal for moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as state instrument and moral discipline (Roman model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Roman religion, "though an admirable system of moral discipline, was never an independent source of moral enthusiasm. It was the creature of the State..." It established oaths, filial/paternal authority, marriage solemnities, and patriotic feeling, but was primarily selfish—a means to prosperity and averting calamity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for judging religious moral influence: whether religion inspires independent moral enthusiasm or functions instrumentally to enforce social order and private advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epicureanism's evaluative role: negative/anti-patriotic tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Epicureanism is characterised as primarily negative in the Roman context—'chiefly negative. The anti-patriotic tendency of its teaching contributed to that destruction of national feeling...'—and generally unfit as a constructive ethic for a martial, patriotic society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess the social adequacy of an ethical system: an ethic emphasizing ease and pleasure may undermine collective virtues required by certain social orders and thus be judged deficient in those contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posthumous reputation as a moral motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Among Roman moralists the 'desire for reputation, and especially for posthumous reputation—that "last infirmity of noble minds"—assumed an extraordinary prominence' as a spring of heroism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative dimension: reputation (including posthumous fame) functions as a motivating standard for virtue in societies lacking strong theological motives; moral systems may be judged by how they mobilise such motives.
